articles.title: Finding safer water
articles.summary: Where to look for water and what to avoid.

sections.title: Safest first
items: Sealed bottled or packaged water.
Tap water, if local authorities say it is safe.
Water from a protected handpump, tube well or covered well.
Rainwater collected straight into a clean container.
Flowing water from a stream or river, upstream of villages and animals.

sections.title: Avoid
items: Flood water: it often contains sewage and chemicals.
Water near toilets, drains, factories, fields sprayed with pesticide, or dead animals.
Still, stagnant ponds with scum or a strange smell or colour.

sections.title: Always
items: Treat water from any source except sealed bottles before drinking. See Filtration versus disinfection.
Use treated water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and washing food.

references.title: Drinking-water fact sheet
Making Water Safe in an Emergency
references.publisher: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

articles.title: Filtration versus disinfection
articles.summary: Making water safer to drink.

sections.title: The difference
items: Filtering through cloth, sand or a ceramic filter removes dirt but does not reliably kill germs.
Disinfecting by boiling, chlorine tablets or sunlight kills most germs.
For cloudy water, do both: settle, filter, then disinfect.

sections.title: Make water safer
items: Let cloudy water stand so dirt settles, then pour off the clear water.
Strain it through a clean, folded cotton cloth.
Boil it at a full rolling boil for 1 minute. Above about 2,000 m altitude, boil for 3 minutes.
Cool it covered, and store it in a clean, covered container.

sections.title: If you cannot boil
items: Use water purification tablets or drops, following the packet for dose and waiting time.
Solar disinfection: fill clear plastic (PET) bottles of 2 litres or less with clear water and leave them in full sun for at least 6 hours, or 2 days if it is cloudy.

sections.title: Limits
items: Boiling and tablets do not remove chemicals such as fuel, pesticides or industrial waste. Find another source.
Solar disinfection does not work for cloudy water or on days of continuous rain.

articles.title: Safe water storage
articles.summary: Keeping treated water clean.

sections.title: How to store
items: Use clean containers with a tight lid, ideally with a tap or narrow neck.
Pour water out instead of dipping cups or hands in.
Keep containers off the floor, out of sunlight and away from fuel and chemicals.
Label containers with the date you filled them.

sections.title: How much
items: Plan at least 3 litres per person per day for drinking and cooking, and more in hot weather.
Washing and hygiene need much more; store extra when you can.

sections.title: Keeping it fresh
items: Replace water you stored yourself about every 6 months.
Use sealed bottled water before its expiry date.

articles.title: Dehydration warning signs
articles.summary: When fluid loss becomes dangerous.

sections.title: Early signs
items: Thirst and a dry mouth.
Dark yellow urine or peeing less.
Tiredness, headache or dizziness.

sections.title: Danger signs
items: Confusion, fainting or a racing heartbeat.
No urine for 8 hours or more.
Sunken eyes, or a sunken soft spot on a baby's head.

sections.title: What to do
items: Drink small amounts often. Use oral rehydration salts for diarrhoea or vomiting.
See First Aid › Dehydration for full steps.

articles.title: Basic emergency shelter
articles.summary: Staying dry, out of the wind and off cold ground.

sections.title: Priorities
items: Get out of rain, wind and direct sun.
Insulate yourself from the ground with dry leaves, cardboard, mats or spare clothes.
Use existing safe structures before building one.

sections.title: Choosing a spot
items: Low ground, dry riverbeds and stream banks that can flood suddenly.
Under dead trees, loose rocks, damaged buildings or power lines.

sections.title: Danger
items: Never use charcoal, stoves, heaters or generators inside a closed shelter or tent. Carbon monoxide can kill without warning.

references.title: Disaster awareness guidance (Do's and Don'ts)

articles.title: Staying warm
articles.summary: Holding on to body heat in cold or wet conditions.

sections.title: Do
items: Wear several loose layers rather than one thick one.
Cover your head, neck, hands and feet.
Change out of wet clothes as soon as you can.
Eat and drink regularly; warm drinks help.
Huddle together to share warmth.

sections.title: Avoid
items: Alcohol: it makes you lose heat faster.
Sitting or lying directly on cold ground.
Burning fuel indoors without good ventilation.

sections.title: Watch for
items: Uncontrolled shivering, confusion or slurred speech. See First Aid › Hypothermia.

references.title: Disaster awareness guidance (Do's and Don'ts)

articles.title: Managing extreme heat
articles.summary: Staying safe during heatwaves.

sections.title: Do
items: Drink water regularly, even if you are not thirsty.
Stay indoors or in shade during the hottest hours, especially around noon to 3 pm.
Wear light, loose cotton clothes and cover your head outdoors.
Use ORS, buttermilk, lassi, lemon water or rice water to replace salts.
Check on older people, children, and anyone ill or living alone.

sections.title: Avoid
items: Heavy work in the afternoon sun.
Alcohol, and large amounts of tea, coffee or fizzy drinks.
Leaving children or animals in parked vehicles, even briefly.

sections.title: Watch for
items: Confusion, very hot skin or collapse are signs of heatstroke. Call 112.

references.title: Disaster awareness guidance (Do's and Don'ts)
National Action Plan on Heat Related Illnesses
references.publisher: National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India

articles.title: Storms and floods
articles.summary: Before, during and after cyclones, storms and floods.

sections.title: Before
items: Follow official warnings from the India Meteorological Department and local authorities.
Charge phones and power banks and keep your emergency kit ready.
Move important documents and medicines to a high, dry place.
Know the way to higher ground or the nearest shelter.

sections.title: During
items: Move to higher ground if water is rising.
Stay indoors away from windows during a cyclone. A sudden calm may be the eye of the storm; stay inside.
Switch off electricity and gas at the mains if told to, or if water is entering and it is safe.

sections.title: Never
items: Walk or drive through flood water. Shallow moving water can knock you over and sweep a car away.
Touch electric poles, fallen wires or wet electrical equipment.
Shelter under trees or stand in open fields during lightning.

sections.title: After
items: Return home only when authorities say it is safe.
Treat all water before drinking and throw away food touched by flood water.

references.title: Disaster awareness guidance (Do's and Don'ts)

articles.title: Earthquakes
articles.summary: Drop, cover and hold on.

sections.title: During shaking
items: Drop to your hands and knees.
Take cover under a sturdy table or desk, or against an inside wall, and protect your head and neck.
Hold on until the shaking stops.
If outdoors, move to an open area away from buildings, trees and power lines.

sections.title: Do not
items: Run outside while the ground is shaking.
Use lifts.
Stand near windows, shelves or heavy furniture.

sections.title: After
items: Expect aftershocks.
Check for gas leaks by smell and do not use flames or switches if you suspect one.
Leave damaged buildings and stay out until they are declared safe.

references.title: Disaster awareness guidance (Do's and Don'ts)

articles.title: Basic evacuation preparation
articles.summary: Being ready to leave quickly.

sections.title: Get ready
items: Know at least two ways out of your area and where official shelters are.
Agree a meeting point and one contact outside the area that everyone will call or message.
Keep a go-bag ready (see Preparedness › Evacuation checklist).
Keep fuel in your vehicle above half a tank during warnings, if you have one.

sections.title: When told to leave
items: Leave early. Roads get blocked as conditions worsen.
Switch off electricity, gas and water if authorities advise it.
Lock your home and tell your contact where you are going.
Follow official routes. Do not take shortcuts through flooded or blocked areas.

articles.title: Using a compass
articles.summary: Taking and following a direction.

sections.title: Follow a bearing
items: Hold the phone flat and level, away from metal, magnets and vehicles.
Point the top of the phone at your target and read the heading.
Pick a landmark in that direction, walk to it, then repeat.

sections.title: Good to know
items: Phone compasses need calibration; move the phone in a figure 8 if readings jump.
Magnetic north differs slightly from true north. HAVEN can show true north when it has a GPS fix.

articles.title: Reading maps
articles.summary: Matching a map to what you see.

sections.title: Steps
items: Turn the map so north on the map points north.
Find two or three features you can see, such as a road, river, railway or hill.
Locate them on the map to work out where you are.
Plan a route along clear features such as roads or rivers rather than across open country.
Check your position regularly against landmarks.

sections.title: Offline
items: Download map regions in HAVEN before you travel.

articles.title: Finding and recording GPS coordinates
articles.summary: Knowing and sharing exactly where you are.

sections.title: Steps
items: Open Tools › GPS coordinates and wait until the accuracy number is small.
Write down latitude and longitude together with the time.
Attach the location to a note in the Field Notebook for places you need to find again.

sections.title: Good to know
items: GPS works without mobile data, but needs a view of the sky.
Five decimal places locate you to about a metre.
Read numbers slowly and repeat them back when giving them over the phone.

articles.title: Morse SOS and distress signals
articles.summary: Signalling for help with light, sound or marks.

sections.title: SOS
items: SOS is three short, three long, three short: ··· ––– ···, sent without gaps and then repeated.
Use Signal & Light to flash it with the torch or screen, or sound it.

sections.title: Other signals
items: Three of anything is a recognised distress signal: three whistle blasts, three flashes or three fires in a triangle.
By day, flash sunlight from a mirror or shiny surface towards aircraft or searchers.
On the ground, make large shapes in contrasting material. A V means you need help; an X means you need medical help.

sections.title: Tips
items: Light signals carry far at night. Save battery by signalling when you can see or hear searchers.

references.title: Ground-to-air visual signal code (Annex 12, Search and Rescue)

articles.title: Navigation without mobile data
articles.summary: Getting around when there is no signal.

sections.title: Before you go
items: Download HAVEN map regions for where you are going.
Save key places (homes, hospitals, shelters) as notes with locations.
Write important numbers and addresses on paper too.

sections.title: On the way
items: Use GPS coordinates and the compass to check your direction.
Follow roads and named landmarks.
In unfamiliar country, staying put where people expect you is often safer than walking out.

articles.title: Basic route preparation
articles.summary: Planning a trip so others can find you.

sections.title: Steps
items: Tell someone your route and when you expect to arrive.
Set a safety check-in in HAVEN.
Check weather warnings.
Download offline maps for the whole route.
Carry water, snacks, a torch and a charged power bank.
Note fuel, food and medical stops along the way.

articles.title: Emergency ration planning
articles.summary: Stocking food that keeps and is easy to prepare.

sections.title: Principles
items: Store foods your household already eats and knows how to cook.
Keep enough ready-to-eat food for at least the first three days.
Choose foods that need little water or fuel, such as sattu, poha, roasted chana, peanuts and biscuits.
Use and replace stock in date order so nothing expires.

sections.title: Plan quantities
items: Use Guides › Emergency Cookbook › Ration and water planner to work out how much you need.

references.title: Build a Kit and Make a Plan

articles.title: Emergency kit checklist
articles.summary: A bag of essentials ready to grab.

sections.title: Pack
items: Drinking water
Ready-to-eat food
Torch and spare batteries
Charged power bank and cables
First-aid kit
Personal medicines for at least a week
Copies of ID and important documents in a waterproof pouch
Some cash in small notes
Whistle
Battery or wind-up radio
Matches or lighter in a waterproof container
Rain cover and a warm layer
Soap, sanitiser and sanitary products
Masks
Blanket or emergency foil blanket
Phone numbers written on paper
Items for babies, older people or pets

references.title: Build a Kit and Make a Plan

articles.title: Food storage safety
articles.summary: Keeping stored food safe to eat.

sections.title: Do
items: Keep food in sealed containers in a cool, dry place off the floor.
Store food away from fuel, pesticides and cleaning products.
Use older stock first and check dates regularly.

sections.title: Throw away
items: Food that has touched flood water, unless it is in an undamaged sealed can.
Cans that are bulging, leaking, badly dented or rusted.
Anything that smells, looks or feels wrong. When in doubt, throw it out.

references.title: Food Safety in a Power Outage and Flood
references.publisher: US Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service

articles.title: Battery and power management
articles.summary: Making your phone last.

sections.title: Save battery
items: Turn on battery saver.
Lower screen brightness and close apps you do not need.
Switch to airplane mode when you do not need a signal. GPS can still work.
Switch the phone on at agreed times to check messages.
Keep the phone warm in cold weather; cold drains batteries fast.

sections.title: Charging
items: Keep power banks charged and rotate spare batteries.
A vehicle charger or small solar panel can help during long outages.

sections.title: Never
items: Run a generator indoors or in a closed garage.

references.title: Build a Kit and Make a Plan

articles.title: Preparing supplies before a journey
articles.summary: What to carry when you travel.

sections.title: Carry
items: Water
Snacks
Offline maps downloaded
Charged phone and power bank
Torch
Personal medicines
Small first-aid kit
ID and some cash
Emergency numbers on paper
Warm or rain layer
Route shared with someone

articles.title: What to do when lost
articles.summary: Stop, think, observe, plan.

sections.title: Steps
items: Stop. Sit down and stay calm.
Think about how you got here and who knows your plans.
Observe: check GPS, landmarks, water, shelter and the time of day.
Plan: if people know your route, stay where you are and make yourself easy to find.

sections.title: Get found
items: Share your coordinates by SMS if you have any signal; texts get through more often than calls.
Use bright clothing, the torch or three whistle blasts to signal.
Find shelter before dark and ration water.

articles.title: Roadside emergencies
articles.summary: Breakdowns and crashes on the road.

sections.title: Steps
items: Pull as far off the road as you can and turn on hazard lights.
Get everyone out on the side away from traffic and stand well back, behind a barrier if there is one.
Place a warning triangle well behind the vehicle if it is safe to do so.
Call 112 for injuries or danger. On national highways, the highway helpline is 1033.

sections.title: At a crash
items: Do not move injured people unless there is fire or other immediate danger.
Do not smoke or use flames near leaking fuel.

articles.title: Nighttime visibility
articles.summary: Being seen and seeing at night.

sections.title: Do
items: Wear light-coloured or reflective clothing.
Carry a torch, or use the phone light or screen light in HAVEN.
Walk facing oncoming traffic, well off the road.
Use well-lit routes where possible.

articles.title: Safety check-ins
articles.summary: Letting someone know you are okay.

sections.title: How to use them
items: Agree with a trusted person what they should do if you miss a check-in.
Start a check-in in SOS › Safety check-in before you set off.
Tap I'm safe when you arrive, or extend it if you are delayed.

sections.title: Note
items: HAVEN alerts you when time runs out and can prepare a message for you to send. It never sends anything on its own.

articles.title: Communicating location to trusted contacts
articles.summary: Making sure people can find you.

sections.title: Steps
items: Open SOS and wait for a location with good accuracy.
Send it to a contact by SMS. Short texts get through on weak signal.
Add a landmark, such as a temple, school or shop name.
Say how accurate the fix is and when it was taken.

sections.title: Remember
items: Opening the messaging app does not send the message. Check it was sent.

articles.title: Power-outage checklist
articles.summary: Getting ready for long power cuts.

sections.title: Checklist
items: Torches and spare batteries in an easy place
Power banks charged
Water stored
Food that needs no refrigeration
Fridge and freezer kept closed
Medicines needing cold storage planned for
Sensitive appliances unplugged
Generators only used outdoors, away from windows

references.title: Build a Kit and Make a Plan

articles.title: Evacuation checklist
articles.summary: What to do before you leave home.

sections.title: Checklist
items: Go-bag packed
Documents and medicines packed
Phones and power banks charged
Meeting point and outside contact agreed
Electricity, gas and water switched off if advised
Pets and their food ready
Home locked
Route and destination shared with your contact

references.title: Disaster awareness guidance (Do's and Don'ts)

articles.title: Household emergency plan
articles.summary: Agreeing what everyone will do.

sections.title: Plan
items: Emergency contacts saved in HAVEN and written on paper
A meeting point near home and one outside the area
One contact outside the area everyone will message
Who collects children from school
Who helps older or disabled family members
Where the mains switches and gas valve are
Where the emergency kit is kept
When the plan was last practised

Safety check-in set
